title: Standard Fire Insurance Co. v. Knowles (2013)
summary: A pre-certification stipulation by the named plaintiff did not cap the absent class members’ claims for CAFA jurisdiction.
notes: This assigned note addresses the effect of the stipulation. The full CAFA jurisdictional requirements and exceptions require separate analysis.

sections.Parties: Knowles sought to represent a class in a suit against an insurance company.
sections.Material Facts: The named plaintiff filed in state court and purported to limit the class’s recovery below the federal Class Action Fairness Act threshold. The class had not yet been certified, so the absent members had not been bound to that limitation through an authorized representative proceeding.
sections.Procedural History: The jurisdictional dispute reached the Supreme Court in connection with removal. The Court rejected the stipulation as a means of controlling the class-wide amount.
sections.Issue: Could the named plaintiff’s stipulation prevent CAFA jurisdiction by limiting all class damages before certification?
sections.Holding: No. It could not bind absent class members and therefore did not establish the proposed limit on their claims.
sections.Reasoning: The decision turned on representative authority. A person may limit a claim the person controls, but cannot reduce the claims of absentees before acquiring authority to act for them. The aggregate jurisdictional analysis therefore could not assume that the proposed stipulation actually constrained the entire class.

learning.why: A pre-certification stipulation by the named plaintiff did not cap the absent class members’ claims for CAFA jurisdiction.

topics.cp-cafa: The named plaintiff could not defeat the aggregate jurisdictional amount by stipulating for an uncertified class.
topics.cp-adequate-representation: Before certification the representative lacked authority to bind absent persons to the damages limitation.

mnemonic.rationale: Stipulating the class below five million
